opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The fundamental problem, as I see it, is matching an intent to the right information, out of an enormous, messy, constantly changing body of content, very quickly. That has always been the core of search. What's changing now is who is doing the asking.

For roughly twenty-five years, web search was built for a human sitting at a keyboard. That shaped everything. You assume the person types two or three words. You assume they'll look at ten blue links, maybe click one or two, and do the final work of reading and synthesizing themselves. So the engine optimizes for ranking. It's trying to get the best few results into the top few slots, because human attention is the scarce resource. A whole economy grew up around that: ads, SEO, the whole incentive structure of the open web.

When the consumer of search is an AI agent, a lot of those assumptions break. An agent doesn't type three words. It can express a very rich, detailed intent, a paragraph describing exactly what it needs and why. It doesn't get tired after the first page. It can read a lot of content, but tokens and context windows still cost something, so what it really wants is the most relevant, information-dense pieces of the web, not a page of links designed to get a click. And it needs to be able to trust what it gets back. It needs to know where the information came from, how fresh it is, and how confident it should be, because it's going to take actions based on it.

So for me the fundamental problem has three parts. First, you have to have the web. That means crawling, indexing, and keeping it fresh at real scale, which is hard engineering that doesn't go away. Second, you have to understand intent much more deeply than keyword matching or even traditional semantic retrieval, because the queries are now far more expressive. Third, you have to return results in a form a machine can actually use: precise, attributable, and verifiable.

There's also a bigger question underneath all of this that I care about a lot. If agents become the main way people access the web, what happens to the incentives for people to keep creating and publishing content? The old bargain was that search sent you traffic. If agents read everything and nobody clicks, that bargain breaks. So I think part of building search for this era is helping design a healthy economic model for the open web, so it stays open and keeps getting better, rather than collapsing into a handful of walled gardens.

r001.rationale: It mentions crawling and indexing the web, but does not explain that pages are collected before queries arrive to avoid fetching them at query time.

r002.rationale: It describes matching intent to information and discusses large-scale web content, but does not frame search as a billion-to-billion matching problem between pages and queries accumulated over time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the fundamental problem of web search has always been one of compression and intermediation. There is this enormous, messy, constantly changing corpus out there, and a person shows up with a few words that only partially express what they actually want. The engine's job is to bridge that gap: to understand the intent behind the query, understand what every page on the web is actually about, and then match the two in a few hundred milliseconds.

For a long time the hard part was the matching. You had to crawl and index everything, figure out which pages were authoritative, and rank them well enough that the answer was somewhere in the first few links. The user did the last mile themselves. They clicked, they read, they synthesized across tabs, they came back and refined the query. The search engine was really a very good librarian pointing you to shelves.

What has changed with language models is that the last mile is now something the system can do. So the problem shifts from "return the most relevant documents" to "do the work the user was going to do with those documents." That sounds like a small change, but it reframes everything. Relevance stops being the end goal and becomes an input. The real question becomes: given this intent, what information do I need to go find, how do I verify it, and how do I assemble it into something the person can act on?

And that brings in a bunch of problems that classic search could mostly sidestep. Freshness matters more, because you are no longer just surfacing a page, you are making a claim. Grounding matters more, because a confident wrong answer is worse than a mediocre list of links. And the economics change, because reading and reasoning over content is far more expensive per query than retrieving an index entry, so you have to be smart about when to go deep and when to stay shallow.

So if I had to compress it: the fundamental problem is turning an underspecified human need into a correct, well-sourced answer, at web scale, fast enough that it feels instant. The ingredients were always there. What is new is that the machine can finally close the loop.

r001.rationale: The response mentions crawling and indexing the web, but does not say this happens before queries arrive or that it avoids fetching pages at query time.

r002.rationale: It describes matching queries to pages, but does not communicate a billion-to-billion scale or that queries accumulate over time.

astra-6.text:
I think the fundamental problem is connecting what someone wants to know with the information on the web that will help them. And neither side of that is particularly clean. The user gives you a few words, which are an imperfect expression of their intent. The web gives you this enormous collection of documents, with varying quality, credibility, and freshness.

So the challenge isn’t simply finding pages that contain those words. It’s understanding the need behind the query, finding relevant information, and deciding what deserves the user’s attention. You have to do that quickly, even for questions you’ve never seen before.

r001.rationale: The response describes matching queries to web information, but does not say pages are collected and indexed before queries arrive to avoid fetching them at query time.

r002.rationale: It mentions an enormous collection of documents and user queries, but does not frame search as matching billions of pages against billions of queries accumulated over time.

sol-6.1.text:
At a fundamental level, a search engine is trying to connect what someone wants to know with information that exists on the web. Neither side is particularly clean. The user gives you a few words, which are an imperfect expression of their intent, and the web contains an enormous amount of information of varying quality.

So the problem is more than finding documents that contain those words. It’s understanding the intent behind the query, discovering which information is relevant and trustworthy, and presenting it in a way that helps the person accomplish what they came to do. And you have to do that very quickly, while both the information and people’s needs are constantly changing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses finding relevant web information but does not say pages are collected and indexed before queries arrive to avoid fetching them at query time.

r002.rationale: It describes connecting user intent with web information, but does not frame search as matching billions of pages with billions of queries accumulated over time.
